label: Intro
title: Tagalog and the Filipino people
summary: Where the language comes from, how it became the national language, and the people who speak it
goals: Know how Tagalog relates to Pilipino and Filipino
Understand where many Tagalog words come from
Know why Tagalog was chosen as the basis of the national language
Learn the Filipino character traits that shape how Tagalog is used

blocks.t: A **living language** is one that is "currently in use or valid". It is alive, dynamic and vibrant. Tagalog is a living language.

Tagalog is the basis of the national language of the Philippines. The **1987 Constitution** (Article XIV, Section 6) states: *"The national language of the Philippines is Filipino. As it evolves, it shall be further developed and enriched on the basis of existing Philippine and other languages."*
Filipino keeps growing as new words, concepts and ideas come in through technology, changing lifestyles, globalisation, contact with foreign cultures, and the media.

head: Name
What it means
rows: the language of the Tagalog regions (Katagalugan), from central to southern Luzon
the name for the Tagalog-based national language, introduced in 1961
the national language today, as named in the 1987 Constitution
blocks.title: Three names

blocks.t: Tagalog has very ancient roots going back thousands of years. It even had its own writing system, **Alibata**, also known as **Baybayin**, a Sanskritic alphabet in which each sign stood for a syllable (ba, ka, da, ga…).

Tagalog and the other Philippine languages belong to the Malayan branch of the great **Malayo-Polynesian** or **Austronesian** family. Its hundreds of languages spread from Taiwan through the Philippines to Hawaii, Fiji and New Zealand, and across Indonesia and the Malay peninsula to Madagascar.

head: Source
What came from it
rows: about 150 terms used in Philippine languages, especially names of plants and animals
381 words about food, abstract ideas, metal smithing, kinship, agriculture, business, tools, industries and games
a few words that came with Islam; many fell out of use in Tagalog-speaking areas
a great deal: religious, governmental, social, legal and abstract terms, and words for foreign articles and luxuries (plus a few Mexican words)
words with no exact equivalent, brought in with American education and government
no words, despite the occupation in the 1940s
blocks.title: Words borrowed over the centuries
The structure stayed the same
blocks.t: After all these contacts, the **construction** of Tagalog was not influenced by the colonisers' languages. It kept its essentially Malayo-Polynesian structure. That is why its grammar works so differently from English.

blocks.title: Good news for English speakers
blocks.t: Because of Spanish and English loanwords, you already half know a lot of Tagalog words. Lesson 1 shows how to decode them: **kompyúter** is computer and **títser** is teacher.

sections.title: How Tagalog became the national language

blocks.t: The Philippines had **172 languages**, three of them already extinct. Eight major languages (Tagalog, Cebuano, Ilocano, Hiligaynon, Bicolano, Waray, Kapampangan and Pangasinan) belong to the Malayo-Polynesian family, but **no two are mutually comprehensible**. In the 1980s they were spoken by 90% of the population.
President Manuel L. Quezon proclaimed a national language based on Tagalog on **December 31, 1937**. Tagalog was chosen for these reasons:

head: Reason
Details
rows: Spoken across 10 major provinces and parts of Marinduque and Mindoro
Unlike the Visayan languages; Tagalog variations are understood by all native speakers
More books are written and published in Tagalog than in any other native language
The capital, where the major government offices are

head: Year
Event
rows: Quezon proclaims a national language based on Tagalog
The national language is introduced in schools
Independence; the national language becomes an official language
President Magsaysay proclaims Linggo ng Wika (National Language Week)
The Constitution names the national language Filipino
blocks.title: Milestones
How many speak it
items: By the 2000 census, around 29% of Filipinos spoke Tagalog as their first language.
About 65% spoke or understood it with varying degrees of skill.
Today Filipino is taught in schools and used on radio, television, in print, songs and church services.

blocks.t: Learning Tagalog is more enjoyable and meaningful when you understand the culture and the people. Filipinos are known for their warmth and hospitality. They are friendly, loving and caring, and they keep their sense of humour even in a crisis.

head: Strengths of the Filipino character
rows: Pakikipagkapwa-tao (a basic sense of justice and concern for others)
blocks.title: From a 1998 study

blocks.t: The same study listed weaknesses too: extreme personalism, extreme family centredness, lack of discipline, passivity, colonial mentality, the **kanya-kanya** syndrome (to each his own), and lack of analysis and self-reflection.

blocks.title: Things to watch for
items: A relaxed attitude to time (coming late, missed deadlines, programmes starting late) puzzles many foreigners, and also irritates Filipinos who are punctual.
Learn to read body language. What do people really mean when they say yes, no or perhaps?
Respect for elders runs through the language, as you will see with pô in Lesson 3.

blocks.title: How long it takes
blocks.t: The textbook plans three months of intensive study, then three more months of speaking practice for at least two hours a day. After about 250 hours, an average learner should speak, write and understand simple, everyday Tagalog.

exercises.q: Match each word to its meaning.

recap: Tagalog is the basis of Filipino, the national language (called Pilipino from 1961).
It is a Malayo-Polynesian language that borrowed words from Sanskrit, Chinese, Arabic, Spanish and English, but kept its own structure.
It was chosen because it is widely spoken, not split into dialects, rich in literature, the language of Manila, and the language of the Revolution.
Filipinos value concern for others, family, joy and humour. Learn to read body language and expect a relaxed attitude to time.
